quizzes.title: Checkpoint 1 — The Web Stack
quizzes.intro: Check whether you understand browsers, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes HTML’s primary role?
questions.explanation: HTML describes structure and meaning so browsers and assistive technologies can interpret content.

wrongExplanations.a: Presentation is mainly CSS. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.c: Secrets must not live in HTML. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.d: Packet routing is networking, not HTML. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.

questions.prompt: After receiving HTML, a browser typically:

options.text: Parses HTML, fetches assets, applies CSS, runs JS, and paints the page
Turns the page into a SQL table automatically

questions.explanation: Browsers parse markup, request linked assets, style content, execute scripts, and render pixels.

wrongExplanations.a: Linked CSS/JS are part of normal loading. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.c: HTML is not auto-converted into SQL tables. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.d: Rendering does not upload password vaults. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.

questions.prompt: Semantic HTML is important because it:

options.text: Forces every site to look identical
Improves accessibility, maintainability, and meaning beyond visuals

questions.explanation: Semantic elements communicate structure to people and tools, which helps accessibility and maintenance.

wrongExplanations.a: Semantics do not force one visual design. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.c: HTTPS is separate transport security. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.d: Semantics do not disable JavaScript. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.

questions.prompt: Which CSS tool is generally best for true two-dimensional layouts?
questions.explanation: CSS Grid is built for row-and-column layout together.

wrongExplanations.a: Floats are a weaker legacy approach for complex layouts.
wrongExplanations.c: Blink is obsolete and unrelated. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.d: Status codes are HTTP metadata. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.

options.text: Information that can change and drive what the UI shows

questions.explanation: State is mutable information such as selected items, open menus, or form values.

wrongExplanations.a: That is geography, not UI state. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.c: DNS maps names to addresses. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.d: A reset is styling, not app state. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.

quizzes.title: Checkpoint 2 — Forms, Access, APIs
quizzes.intro: Apply forms, accessibility, responsive design, and fetching.

questions.prompt: Client-side form validation alone is limited because:

options.text: Users can bypass browser checks, so servers must validate important data

questions.explanation: Client checks help UX, but authoritative validation must happen on the server.

wrongExplanations.a: Validation can be implemented accessibly. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.c: Labels remain required good practice. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.d: Validation does not block CSS. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.

options.text: Relying on color alone for errors
Using semantic HTML, keyboard access, and meaningful labels/alternatives

questions.explanation: Accessible experiences need structure, operable controls, and clear text.

wrongExplanations.a: Color-only cues exclude some users. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.c: Focus visibility matters for keyboard users. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.d: Vague link text fails out of context. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.

options.text: Design only for desktops then crush the layout
Start from a usable small layout, then enhance at larger breakpoints
Create a separate domain for phones always

questions.explanation: Mobile-first begins with constrained layouts and progressively enhances.

wrongExplanations.a: Desktop-first shrinkage is often fragile. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.c: Grid works well responsively. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.d: Separate domains are rarely required. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.

questions.prompt: Production API UI code should usually handle:

options.text: Loading, empty, success, and failure states

questions.explanation: Network requests fail and return empty results; resilient UI plans for those cases.

wrongExplanations.a: Happy-path-only code breaks in production. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.c: Secrets in URLs are unsafe. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.d: Status codes are essential signals. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.

questions.prompt: Why is assigning untrusted HTML with innerHTML risky?

options.text: It can enable XSS if malicious markup executes

questions.explanation: Untrusted HTML can introduce hostile script/markup; prefer safe text APIs when possible.

wrongExplanations.a: Unsafe HTML is not an SEO strategy. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.c: CSS is not permanently deleted. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.d: Acceptance is not the same as safety. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.

quizzes.title: Final Quiz — Web Judgment
quizzes.intro: Use the whole lesson. Focus on engineering judgment.

questions.prompt: A page is blank with no clear layout. Best first step?

options.text: Inspect Console/Network evidence and isolate the failure

questions.explanation: Evidence-first debugging identifies JS errors, failed requests, or DOM/CSS issues quickly.

wrongExplanations.a: Rewrites without diagnosis waste time. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.c: Disabling HTTPS is unsafe and irrelevant. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.d: Semantic HTML is not the villain. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.

questions.prompt: Which choice reflects professional fundamentals on a landing page?

options.text: Ignore keyboard users if mouse works
Use semantic structure, responsive layout, and a clear primary action
Ship an uncompressed 5MB hero by default
Embed API secret keys in frontend JS

questions.explanation: Professionals combine meaning, responsiveness, clarity, and safety. That distinction is central to applying the lesson correctly.

wrongExplanations.a: Keyboard access is part of quality. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.c: Huge images hurt performance. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.d: Frontend secrets are visible to users. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.

questions.prompt: Flexbox is usually best when you need:

options.text: One-dimensional alignment in a row/column (nav, button group, card footer)

questions.explanation: Flexbox excels at one-dimensional distribution and alignment. That distinction is central to applying the lesson correctly.

wrongExplanations.a: Grid is generally better for true 2D page grids.
wrongExplanations.c: Databases are unrelated to Flexbox. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.d: DNS is networking infrastructure. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.

options.text: If JavaScript fails, the page may be useless
Start with a usable HTML/CSS baseline, then add richer behavior
Ship broken HTML and patch with ads

questions.explanation: A usable baseline keeps content available even when scripts fail.

wrongExplanations.a: That attitude is the opposite of progressive enhancement.
wrongExplanations.c: Broken foundations are not a strategy. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.d: The web is multi-browser. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.

questions.prompt: Mature web thinking treats accessibility and performance as:

options.text: Core product quality alongside features and security

questions.explanation: Quality attributes are requirements, not afterthoughts. That distinction is central to applying the lesson correctly.

wrongExplanations.a: Accessibility is not optional polish. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.c: Frameworks still need fundamentals. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
wrongExplanations.d: Payments need server-side enforcement. Choose the option that matches the lesson’s core idea instead.
